But if the camp shall fight against me, deaf to my warning,
no longer, my sons, will I delay you and the sweet
house of Assaracus's race, nor shall wounded Rome see
Paulus returning like Varro.'
So then with divided mind the troubled leaders sought
their camp. But already on the foretold fields had settled
the Carthaginian, keeping the Aetolian plains for battle.
Never at another time was the Italian land shaken by a greater
host of men, by a greater throng of hoofed beasts beneath arms.
For at once they feared the worst both for their race and their city,
nor was hope of contending given beyond a single Mars.

title: Punica
text:
The sons of Faunus, sacred band, with the Sican as ally,
have rushed to war, the Rutulian who guards the Daunian realm
and rejoices in the Laurentine house and the spring of Numicus,
whom Castrum and Ardea, once grievous to the Phrygians, sent,
whom Lanuvium, Juno's seat sloping from a high ridge,
and Collatia, nurse of chaste Brutus,
and those who love the cruel grove of Trivia, and who love the mouths
of the Tuscan river and cherish Cybele in the warm Almo.
Hence Tibur, your city, Catillus, and Praeneste, dedicated
to Fortune's sacred ridges, and Antemnae, older
than ancient Crustumium, and Labici, fit for the plough.
And those who drink the wave of sceptre-bearing Tiber,
and who hold the banks of the Anio and are watered by the cold
Simbruvium, and tame with mattocks the Aequiculan fields.
Their counsellor was Scaurus—Scaurus then in his tender age,
but already valour, being born for the ages, gave its signs.
It was not their wont to brandish spears in the field,
nor their custom to fill the quiver with feathered arrows:
they choose the javelin and swords handy with short blades;
their heads covered with bronze, they rise above the columns with their crests.
But those whom Setia, set apart for the table of Lyaeus himself,
and Velitrae sent from its unsung valley,
whom Cora, whom Signia, foaming with harsh new wine,
and whom the plague-bearing damp of the Pomptine fields,
where the misty marsh of Satura overflows, and, livid with black
mud, Ufens, turbid through the squalid fields,
gathers his waters and stains the sea with slime—
these Scaevola leads, mighty in ancestors and not unworthy in his right hand
of his forebears, on whose shield is engraved the honoured
likeness of dread glory: fires blaze on the altars,
in the midst of the rampart stands Mucius, his anger
turned upon himself, and valour rages in the image.
†Then the struck image they entered, and the wars by their master
is seen, Porsena fleeing the burning right hand.
Those by whom the Circean ridges and Anxur of the rocky summit
and the Hernican stones are scraped with the pressed ploughshare,
those by whom rich Anagnia is furrowed with crumbling soil,
Sulla led, with the companies of Ferentinum and the Privernates
roused together, and the youth of Sora
glittered, added to the weapons. Here the manhood of Scaptia,
here the throng of Fabrateria, nor was Atina, descending
from its snowy mountain, absent, nor Suessa, worn with wars,
nor Frusino, not unwarlike from the hard plough.
But he who dwells beside the Liris, mingling its sulphurous streams
with the Fibrenus and gliding with silent shallows to the shore,
the Arpinate, with the manhood summoned from Venafrum
and the right hands of the Larinates, bristling, sets in motion
his allied arms and drains huge Aquinum of its men.
Tullius was sweeping into the columns his bronze-clad squadrons,
a royal offspring and blood from high Tullus.
O with how great endowment a youth, and how great a citizen
he will give to the peoples of Ausonia in the ages to come!
He, heard beyond the Ganges, beyond the Indians,
will fill the lands with his voice and curb frenzied wars
with the thunderbolt of his tongue, nor will leave thereafter
any of his descendants to hope for equal glory in eloquence.
Behold among the foremost, of Therapnaean blood from Clausus,
Nero exults, not to be imitated in his swift daring.
Him the cohort of Amiternum, and Casperia, drawing its name
from Bactra, him Foruli and Reate, dedicated to the great
Mother of the heaven-dwellers, and Nursia, dwelt in
by frosts, and the cohorts from the Tetrican crag accompany.
For all, the spear is their glory, and the shield is bent back into a circle,
and their cones are without plumes, and there is covering for the left leg.
They went, and, glad, part were singing with their voice of Sancus,
the founder of their race, part bore on their lips the praises,
Sabus, of you, who first, from your own surname,
called the peoples Sabines with great dominion.

title: Punica
text:
What of him who goads the nurslings of the Picene land,
Curio, bristling both with scales and with a horse-hair crest—
how great a part of the war comes! Not on the upturned sea
so thick whitens the wave in the broken billows,
nor with a lighter gathering, where through a thousand columns the maiden
imitates the lines of Mars with crescent shields,
does both the earth and the Amazonian Thermodon resound.
Here too those whom the rocky fields of Numana pasture,
and those for whom the altars of seacoast Cupra smoke,
and those who guard the Truentine towers with their river,
could be seen: shield-bearing columns far off under the flashing sun
quiver in the clouds with a bloody light.
Ancon stands to dye the distaff, no cheaper in its purple
than Sidon or than Libya, and Hadria stands, moistened by the Vomanus,
and the harsh standard-bearer of shaggy Asculum.
This memorable name Picus once established from high
Saturn, his father, whom Circe with her song
bade fly through the air stripped of his form,
and she sprinkled a saffron glory upon the feathers of the fleeing one.
Before, as fame teaches, the land was held by the Pelasgians,
whose ruler was Aesis, and he left his name to the river
and then called the peoples Asili from himself.
But the country-dwellers strengthened the camp with no worse
strength, the Umbrians coming from their hollow mountains.
These the Aesis and the Sapis wash, and the Metaurus, whirling
his rapid waves with a sounding eddy over the rocks,
and Clitumnus washes the huge bull, bathing it in his sacred stream,
and the Nar, hastening to the Tiber with whitening waves,
and the inglorious water of the Tinia
and the Clanis and the Rubicon and the Sena, named from the Senones.
But the father Albula glides amid them with his huge stream
and grazes the walls with his near-brought bank.
With these the cities Arna and Mevania of the glad meadows,
Hispellum and Narnia, leaning on its hard mountain through the rocks,
and Iguvium, once beset with damp mists,
and Fulginia, lying on the open plain without walls;
with these, brave peoples: the man of Ameria, and Camers, to be praised
for arms or mattocks, with these Sassina, rich
in milk, and the men of Tudertum, not sparing to worship Mars.
Their leader Piso led men scornful of death,
a boy in face and fair in bearing, but with shrewd heart
he matched old age and by craft had surpassed his years.
He shone before the front line in painted arms,
as a fiery gem flashes on the tawny necklace of the Arsacidae.
And now the legion, filled out through the Etruscan companies,
looked to its ruler Galba of the great name.
For him Minos begins the line, and Pasiphae, shut
in the bull, and then in order stand his illustrious fathers.
Chosen men Caere sent, chosen men Cortona, the house
of proud Tarchon, and ancient Graviscae.
And Alsium, the shore dear to Argive Halesus,
and Fregenae, beset by its squalid plain.
There was present too Faesula, interpreter of the lightning with sacred wings,
and the Clusine throng, an old terror to the Roman walls,
when, great Porsena, you bade
the banished Tarquins, in vain, to rule over Rome.
Then those whom Luna sent from its snowy quarries,
distinguished by its harbour, than which no other is more spacious
to receive countless ships and to close in the sea,
and Vetulonia, once the glory of the Maeonian race.
This first gave the twelve fasces to go before,
and joined as many axes with their silent terror.
This adorned the high curule chairs with the honour of ivory
and first edged the robe with Tyrian purple.
This same first brought forth the bronze to kindle battles.
With these mingled the cohort of Nepe and the Aequi Falisci,
and those who hold your hearths, Flavina, and the Sabatian
pools and the Ciminian lake, who frequent the dwellings of Sutrium
not far off and Soracte, sacred to Phoebus.
They bear two darts each: for their heads a cap of wild beast's hide
is caution enough: they condemn the Lycian bows for spears.

title: Punica
text:
These battle-lines knew how to make war. But the Marsian manhood
knew both to make war with the hand and to charm sleep upon water-snakes,
and to dull the viper's tooth with herbs and with song.
They say that Angitia, offspring of Aeetes, first
showed them evil grasses and to master poisons by touch
and to shake the moon from the pole, curbing rivers
with her hissings, and to lay the mountains bare, summoning the woods.
But a more fearful guest gave a name to the peoples,
when Marsyas fled across the seas the Phrygian Crenae,
overcome by Phoebus's plectrum in the Mygdonian flute.
Marruvium, celebrated by the name of old Marrus,
is the head of those cities, and farther in, through the wet
fields, Alba sits and pays back the ears of grain with fruits.
The rest are in the obscurity of fame and without the name of the crowd,
but in number the strongholds are strong. There is joined the fierce
Pelignian, and from cold Sulmo he sweeps his cohorts.
Not lighter than he in wars, the Vestine youth,
hardened by the hunting of beasts, thickened the columns:
this youth shears your citadels, Fiscellus, and green Pinna
and the pastures of Aveia, returning not slowly to their grass.
The Marrucinian too, manhood rivalling the Frentani,
drew the peoples of Corfinium and great Teate.
For all, the boar-spear is borne into battle, for all the slings
wont to bring down the bird from the high sky.
A skin of a bear slain in the hunt covers their breasts.
Nor is the Sidicine cohort wanting. Viriasius arms
a thousand men, surpassed by none either in pitching camp
or in joining a raft and breaking down walls with the hard
ram, and in sending sudden bridges against a tower.
Nor does the Sidicine soldier yield in zeal in his blood,
whom Cales bore. No small founder of the city,
as fame is, was Calais, whom Orithyia, snatched through the air
by Boreas, nursed, a wanderer, in the Getic caves.
But now those whom Campania, rich in wealth, rich in ancestors,
gave to the war from its whole tract,
the Oscans from their neighbouring seats awaited
the coming of their leaders: warm Sinuessa, and the Volturnus,
sounding with its wave, and the towns that silence overthrew, Amyclae,
and Fundi and Caieta, ruled by Lamus, and the home
of Antiphates, hemmed in by the strait, and marshy
Liternum with its pools, and Cyme, once conscious of the fates.
There Nuceria and Gaurus, founded by the seafaring
offspring of Dicarchus, with much Greek soldiery;
there Parthenope and Nola, never penetrable to the Carthaginian,
Allifae and Acerrae, always scorned by the Clanius.
You could see the Sarrastian peoples too and all
the gentle wealth of the Sarnus; there those whom the bays
of Phlegra, rich with sulphur, gathered, Misenus and Baiae,
the Ithacan seat, burning with its Giant's mouth.
Nor was Prochyta absent, nor Inarime, allotted burning
Typhoeus, nor the rocky island of ancient Telon,
nor Calatia of the small walls,
Surrentum and Abella, poor in Ceres's furrow,
and above all Capua—alas, in serene affairs ill-advised
to keep the measure, and doomed to perish by perverse swelling!
Scipio was forming for war the men glad in their ruler.
He had taught the men to surround their breasts with javelin and iron.
Lighter weapons, after the custom of their fathers, they had borne
from home, cornel-shafts burnt to a point without an iron tip;
their use was of the dart and the axe made for the fields.
He himself among them gave great signs of the renown
to come: to brandish the stake, to leap across
the city ditches, to break the watery shoal by swimming
clad in his breastplate: such spectacles of valour
were before the lines. Often, on winged foot,
he himself, on foot, outran the horse, its flanks pierced through,
flying through the open fields; often, the same, towering,
he crossed the breadth of the camp with both stone and spear.
A martial brow and easy hair, nor behind and at the back
was his hair shorter. His eyes blazed with a gentle
aspect, and a pleasing awe was in him for those who beheld him.

title: Punica
text:
The Samnite too was present, his favour not yet leaning
toward the Carthaginians, but neither cleansed of his old anger:
those who reap Batulum and Nucrae, and those who beat
the lairs of Bovianum or cling to the Caudine gorges,
and those whom either Rufrae or Aesernia, or whom
obscure Herdonia sent from its untilled fields.
The Bruttian, not unequal in spirit, and together the youth
roused from the Lucanian ridges and the Hirpinian manhood
bristled with weapons, shaggy with the hides of beasts on their backs.
These the hunt feeds: they have dwelt in lairs and turn their thirst
aside with the river, and their sleep is won by toil.
To these is added the Calabrian and the Sallentine cohorts,
and Brundisium too, where the Italian land ends.
The legion obeyed, entrusted to bold Cethegus,
for whom they reviewed the allied forces and the arms
not distinguished into companies: now the soldier of Leucosia
showed himself from the crags, now the one whom Picentia sent from Paestum
and Cerillae, soon drained by the Punic Mars,
now those whom the Silarus nurses with its waters, in whose stream they say
the hardness of stones grows upon the boughs dipped in.
He praised too the weapons of warlike Salernum,
its scythe-shaped swords, and the oaken clubs, unsmoothed,
which the Buxentian manhood fitted to their right hands.
He himself, bare of shoulder after the native custom of his fathers,
rejoiced in a difficult horse and exercised the strength of his youth
on the hard mouth of the bending steed.
You too, cut down and bereft of your men,
nations of the Eridanus, with no god heeding
your vows then, rushed to the arms that would fall upon you.
Placentia, shaken by war, vied with Mutina,
Mantua vied to send its manhood with Cremona,
Mantua, home of the Muses and lifted to the stars
by Aonian song and a rival of the Smyrnaean lyre.
Then Verona, flowed around by the Athesis, and Faventia, skilled
on every side to nurse the pine that crowns its fields,
Vercellae, and Pollentia, fertile in dark wool,
and the ancient house of Ocnus, once companion of the Trojans
in the Laurentine wars, and Bononia of the little Rhenus,
and those who with heavy oar sluggishly cleave through the muddy waves
the slow pools of marshy Ravenna.
Then the Trojan band, sprung of old from the Euganean
land, and the fugitives from the sacred shores of Antenor.
And Aquileia too overflows with the Veneti's arms.
Then the nimble Ligurian and the Vagenni, scattered among the rocks,
sent hardy descendants to Hannibal's glory.
Their leader Brutus, the greatest confidence of so many peoples,
went and by exhortation kindled them against the well-known foe.
A glad gravity was in the man and a lovable weight of mind
and a valour without gloom. He loved not the thankless praises
of sternness, nor the cloud of the brow,
nor did he seek fame by a perverse path of life.
He had added thrice a thousand men, tried in the arrow's Mars,
the faithful ruler from Sicilian Aetna.
Not so many men did Ilva arm, but men glad to gird on iron,
with its native metal, by which it nurses wars.
He would have forgiven Varro, eager to join battle, whoever
should see at once so many weapons together.
On the Rhoetean shore once with such great hosts
the Leandrian Hellespont saw a thousand ships swarm,
when great Mycenae invaded Troy.
When they came to Cannae, the traces of an ancient city,
they fix their ill-omened standards on the dire rampart.
Nor, with so great a ruin now hanging over the wretched,
did the gods cease to betray the neighbouring disasters.
Through the clear sky the javelins blazed for the astonished companies,
and the high battlements fell from all the rampart,
and Garganus, rushing with nodding summit, laid low the woods,
and Aufidus bellowed, panting from its lowest depths,
and far apart over the great sea the kindled Ceraunian heights
terrified the trembling sailors.
The Calabrian, with the light suddenly withdrawn into measureless
darkness, sought both the land and the shores of Sipus,
and the frequent owl beset the thresholds of the camp.
Nor did the dense clouds of bees cease to wrap themselves
around the alarmed eagles. Not one death-bringing comet,
overthrower of kingdoms, glowed red with flashing hair.
The camp too and the rampart, in the silent night, the raging
beasts broke into, and, snatched before the faces of the trembling,
they scattered the limbs of the joined sentries through the fields.
And when the image of terror mocked their sleep,
the shades of the Gauls were seen to burst from their tombs,
and thrice and four times the Tarpeian rocks, torn from their roots,
trembled deep, and with black blood the river
flowed in the temples of Jove, and tears in great abundance
flowed from the ancient image of father Quirinus.
And the Allia, greater, rose up between its horrid banks.
The Alps did not stay in their place, nor by night or day
did the Apennine stand still amid its huge chasms.
Above the mid heaven, from the Libyan side, flashing
torches came into Latium, and the pole, burst with a din
fearful to hear, and the face of the Thunderer lay open.
Vesuvius too, whirling Aetnean fires from its crags,
thundered, and, with rocks hurled into the clouds,
its Phlegraean summit touched the trembling stars.

title: Punica
text:
Behold, in the midst, a soldier, foreteller of the war, and with face
astonished and senses at once, fills the camp with savage
cries and pants out the disaster to come:
'Spare us, cruel gods. Already the fields fail
with heaps of slaughter. I see the leader of Libya flying
through the dense columns and chariots driven on,
dragging over the arms of men and limbs and standards.
The wind rages with mad whirlwinds and rolls the battles
into our eyes and faces. Unmindful of his age,
Servilius falls, in vain, Trasimene, drawn from your shores.
Where, Varro, do you flee? O Jupiter! by the blow
of a stone Paulus, the last hope, falls upon the weary.
Let the Trebia yield to this destruction. Behold, a bridge
is built of falling bodies, and the smoking Aufidus
casts back the corpses, and the victorious beast tramples the plains.
The man of Agenor bears the axes of the consul after our custom,
and the lictor carries the fasces sprinkled with blood.
Into Libya the pomp of an Ausonian triumph is borne.
O grief! Do you bid us, gods, to have seen even this?
With gold heaped up, whatever is torn from the left hand,
victorious Carthage measures the ruins of Latium.'
9. Latium being troubled by portents, and the gods revealing
through Ausonia the unavailing signs of the disaster to come,
no otherwise than if the omens of the battle to come were favourable
and prosperous, the consul passed the night
sleepless and brandished his weapon in his hand through the shadows,
and now upbraided Paulus for sloth, now made the keen
trumpets sound and longed for the war-call of the night.
Nor was the ardour for a hasty contest less in the Carthaginian.
They burst from the rampart, the sinister Fortune urging them on,
and hands were joined. For the Macae, scattered through the neighbouring
fields to snatch up fodder, poured forth a flying
cloud of weapons. Foremost of all to invade the war,
Mancinus, glad, and first to dye his weapons
with the enemy's blood, falls, and the numerous youth falls.
Nor would Varro have curbed the arms, with the god rebuking him
by the entrails of the beasts and the auspices opposed to Paulus,
had not the lot of the alternate command, by which the camp is ruled,
denied to him, hastening to his fate, the decision of battle.
Yet this availed to grant to the thousands that were to perish
no more than a single day. They returned to the camp, while Paulus
groaned without doubt, who saw that tomorrow's authority
would yield to the madman, and that in vain his men's
lives had been preserved from slaughter. For, turbid with anger
and hostile to delay because of the battle put off, the leader:
'Is it thus, thus,' he said, 'Paulus, that you repay thanks and reward
for your own life? Did they deserve such things, who tore you
from the laws and the urn that menaced you with doom?
Nay, let them at once hand over to the enemy their recalled swords,
let them hand over their arms, command it, or strip them from the right hands of those who fight.
But you, whose eyes and faces I saw wet,
when the consul bade you turn your backs and return,
wait not for the wonted signal of battle to be sought.
Let each, his own leader, snatch his way, when Phoebus
shall begin to sprinkle with his first rays the Gargan summits.
I myself will open the gates in haste. Rush more swiftly, and recall
this day that was snatched from you.' So, turbid, he set the sick
camp ablaze with a deadly love of battle.
But Paulus, now no longer the same in mind or face,
but such as he stood after the battle, on plains strewn
with the soldiery destroyed, with the coming evil hovering
before his eyes and face, as when, the hope of light now taken away,
a lifeless mother is stunned and warms in vain with last
embraces the limbs of her son still warm:
'By the walls of Rome so often shaken,' he said,
'and by these innocent souls, around which the night now flies
with its Stygian shade, spare to go against the disaster.
While the gods' frenzy passes and the anger of Fortune is spent,
the strangeness of Hannibal is enough, if the soldier
learns to bear the name, and looks on the foe without growing cold.
Do you not see, when he is heard of in the neighbouring fields,
how suddenly the blood leaves the pale bodies,
and how the arms fall before the trumpets? The delayer and, as you think,
the feeble Fabius, however many he led into battle
beneath those censured standards, now they take up arms.
But those whom Flaminius—but the gods avert the dire omen.
But if your spirit fights against our warnings and prayers,
open your ears to the god. The Cumaean prophetess sang
these things once through the world, and, foretelling, made known to the lands
your frenzies and yours, in the age of our forefathers.
And now a second prophet to you, in no riddling song, before your face
I sing the fates: if you do not halt tomorrow's standards,
you will confirm with our blood the words of the Phoebean
Sibyl. Nor hereafter shall the fields be made famous by Greek
Diomedes, but, if you persist, by you the consul.'
So Paulus, and tears rose in his burning eyes.

title: Punica
text:
The night too a wicked error defiled.
Satricus, captured by Xanthippus, had endured slavery
on the Libyan shores, and soon among the prizes was given
as a gift to the king of the Autololes for the honour of his valour.
He had a home and twin sons, left behind at Sulmo
at their mother's breast, Mancinus and, together,
Solimus of Rhoetean name. For his stock was Dardanian
and his race from a Phrygian forefather, who, following the sceptre
of Aeneas, had founded a city famous for its walls,
called Solimon after himself. Soon, celebrated by the Italian
colonists, by degrees the name worn down to Sulmo.
But then Satricus, brought with the king amid barbarian troops,
who was not despised, if need required it,
to teach the Gaetulians Latin words as interpreter,
after it was granted him that he might revisit his Pelignian dwelling
and hope for his native hearth, calls the night to his attempt
and stealthily escapes from the unkind camp.
But the man's flight was bare. For, taking up a shield, he avoided
betraying his enterprise, and was returning with his right hand unarmed.
The spoils therefore and the bodies laid low on the field
he searches, and girds himself with the stripped arms of Mancinus.
And now his fear was lighter. But he from whom he bore the spoils
torn from the lifeless one, and whose limbs he had stripped,
was his own son, laid low a little before by the Macan foe.
Behold, at the coming of night and the first slumber,
the other of his sons, Solimus, had carried his steps,
wakeful, over the Ausonian rampart, while by lot in turn
he changed the watches at the gate, and was seeking among the scattered
dead the body of his brother Mancinus, laid low,
desiring to lay the wretched one in stealthy earth.
Nor had he hastened far on his way, when he sees the foe
coming in arms toward the Sidonian mound,
and, with what chance gave unforeseen in sudden straits, in the tomb
of Aetolian Thoas he hides his concealed limbs.
Then, when he sees no arms following more closely behind, and the man
bearing his unaccompanied steps through the shadows,
springing from the mound he hurls his bare javelin
not in vain into his father's back, and Satricus, believing
the band that followed to be Tyrian and the wounds Sidonian,
trembling, looks about for the author of the blind blow.
But when his course brought the victor near with youthful strength,
and the grim light flashed from the familiar arms,
and his brother's shield from afar, the moon betraying it, uncovered
itself before his eyes and the boss gleamed close at hand,
the youth cries out, set ablaze by sudden anger:
'May I not be your offspring, Satricus, born at Sulmo,
nor your brother, Mancinus, and may I confess myself a descendant
unworthy of Pergamean Solimus, if it be granted this man
to escape my hands unpunished. Shall you bear the noble
spoil of my brother before my eyes and carry back, treacherous,
while I breathe, the proud arms of the Pelignian house?
These gifts, dear mother Acca, for the comfort of your grief
I will bring you, to fix forever on your son's tomb.'
Crying out such things, with drawn sword he rushed on.
But from the other now the weapons, now the arms slipped from his hand
when he heard his country and his sons and his wife and the arms named,
and a cold horror had stunned his limbs and his senses.
Then a pitiable voice is poured from his half-dead mouth:
'Spare, I pray, your right hand—not that life may remain to me
(for it is a sin to wish to enjoy this), but with our blood
do not condemn your hands, O son. That captive of Carthage,
now first brought to his native shores,
I am that Satricus, of Solimus's stock. No guilt, my son,
is yours. When you hurled the spear, hot, against me,
I was a Carthaginian. But, escaped from the bitter camp,
I was hastening to you and to the face of my dear wife:
this shield I snatched from the lifeless one. But now, my only one,
carry these arms, excused, back to your brother's tomb.
Yet let it be your first care, son, to bear back
to the leader Paulus the warning: let him strive to draw out the war
and refuse the contests of Mars to the Carthaginian.
He exults in the gods' augury and hopes for measureless
slaughter in the near battle. I beg, restrain the raging
Varro: for the report is that he urges on the standards.
Great enough at this turning-point of my wretched life will be
this solace, to have provided for my own. Now, son, give
to a father found and lost at once the last
kisses.' So speaking, he takes off his helmet and seizes the neck
of his stiffened son with trembling arms:
he labours to heal with words the shame of his son, stunned in mind,
for the wound he has dealt, and to excuse the weapon:
'What witness, what accomplice was present at our deeds?
Did not the night hide the error with its blackening shade?
Why do you tremble? Give, son, give more, give me to join breast to breast.
I, the father myself, absolve your hand, and at the end of my labours
close my eyes with this right hand, I beg.' But the wretched youth,
sighing from the depth of his breast, returns no words or response
to the address, nor any voice, but hastens to stop
the course of the black blood and, weeping, to bind more swiftly
the deep wound with a torn covering.
At last amid his groans the wretched laments broke forth:
'Is it thus, father, that Fortune brings you back to us
in our country? Thus, impious, does she restore you to your son
and your son to his father? O thrice and four times happy
brother, to whom it was given by the fates to recognize his father lost.
But I, unslain by the Sidonians, behold, by my father's
wound recognize my father. Would that at least this, Fortune, had been
a solace for my fault, that you had given me doubtful signs
of my ill-omened race. But it shall be left to the unjust
gods no longer to make our labours criminal.'
While, distraught, he laments these things, now, the blood failing,
the old man had scattered his life into the empty air.
Then the youth, raising his sorrowful face to the stars:
'Witness, daughter of Titan, of my polluted right hand and of the unspeakable
deed, who by your nocturnal light directed my weapons
into my father's body, no longer,' he said,
'shall you be defiled by these eyes and their condemned sight.'
This he says, and at once digs his sword into his breast and, holding up
the black wound, with the flowing blood marks
on the shield his father's charge: FLEE THE BATTLE, VARRO,
and hangs the covering on the point of his uplifted spear
and stretches his limbs over his lamented father.

title: Punica
text:
Such omens of the battle to come the gods were sending
to the Ausonians, and, the shades by degrees departing,
the night, conscious of the crime, yielded to the rosy Dawn.
The Libyan leader called his men to arms, and the Roman to arms
called his after the custom, and for the Carthaginians there returned
a day such as none had ever risen in all the ages.
'You have no need,' said the Carthaginian, 'of goading words,
who from the Herculean pillars to the fields of Iapyx
have measured the road by conquering. Nowhere is spirited Saguntum,
the Alps have yielded, the very proud father of Ausonian waters,
Eridanus, flows down in a captive channel.
The Trebia is sunk with the slaughter of men, and the Lydian mouths
are pressed by Flaminius's tomb, and far and wide the fields
gleam with bones and are furrowed by no ploughshare.
A more illustrious title and a light that will bring more blood
rises. To me, greatness enough, indeed enough and more
than enough be the reward of war: let the rest be conquered
by you. Whatever Rome carried down from the rich Spaniard,
whatever she paraded in her Aetnean triumphs,
nay even whatever, snatched from the Libyan shore,
she stored away, shall come to your swords without casting lots.
Carry home what the right hand shall give. I, your leader, ask
no honour from the spoils. Through the long ages the Dardanian
plunderer shall have stripped for you the world that is now subdued.
You who draw your Sarranian name from a Tyrian origin,
whether the Laurentine land, furrowed by the Sigean farmer,
smiles on you, or whether the Byzacian fields are dearer
to your heart, sprouting with a hundred stalks for Ceres,
I will grant you to choose select fields among the prizes.
I will add too the banks which the Tiber waters with its yellow wave,
to graze far and wide with captive flocks.
But you who, an ally of foreign blood, move my standards
of Byrsa, if you raise a right hand red with Ausonian
slaughter, be from this moment a citizen of Carthage.
And let not Garganus and the shores of Daunus deceive you:
you stand at the walls of Rome. Though the trackless city
is far off and stands distant from our contest,
here today she falls, and beyond this I summon no soldier
to battle: from the battle-line make your course to the Capitol.'
This he says. Then, the defence of the rampart driven forward,
they snatched away the delays of the ditches, and his battle-line
he fits with skill to the place, in order, on the curving banks.
On the left wing for the contest stood the barbarian
warrior Nasamon, and with him the Marmarid, huger of limb,
then the fierce Moor and the Garamantian and the Macae
and the Massylian lines and the throng of the Adyrmachidae,
glad to live by the sword, the people dwelling beside the Nile,
keeping their bodies blackened by the excessive sun.
Their head set over the columns and their command was Nealces.
But on the right, where the Aufidus curves its wave with windings
and wanders around its banks with curving eddy,
Mago rules. The light troops came up whom bristling
Pyrene sent, the peoples, and girded with varied tumult
the river's side: the light-shielded youth gleams,
the Cantabrian before the rest, and the Vasco, his temples uncovered,
and the Balearic, mingling battles with whirled lead,
and the men sprung from the Baetis. Lofty in the centre, he himself
controls the columns, which he strengthened with native soldiery and which
with the troops of the Celts, often steeped in the Eridanus.
But where the river, with its waters slipping back,
withdraws itself and walls the wedges with no defence,
the beast, bearing on its black back turreted masses
and bulwarks, like a moving mound,
nods and lifts up its high walls to the air.
The rest it is granted now to the Numidians, to fly around
and bear their wandering courses and to seethe over the whole field.

title: Punica
text:
While the Libyan, his soldiery kindled, dispenses his forces,
and, insatiable, again and again by exhorting urges
each man by his own deeds, and boasts that he knows
from what right hand come the hissings of the shrieking weapon,
and promises the men that he will fail none as witness,
already Varro, the legion led out of the rampart, was setting in motion
the beginnings of disaster, and, glad, the ferryman over the pale
wave was making room for the shades to come.
The foremost stand still, whom the bloody mark hanging
on the shield forbade to go, and, fixed by the omen, they grow numb.
Beside them a terrible sight: pitiable lay
the bodies in an embrace, and the son, his right hand
laid on his father's breast, covered the deadly wound.
Tears flowed, and thence the grief of Mancinus, brought back
in his brother's death, then the sad augury moved them,
and the face, like a dead man's, on the lifeless body.
Swiftly the fault of the error and the deeds to be lamented
they unfold to the leader, and the arms forbidding battle.
He, burning in spirit: 'Bear all this,' he said, 'to Paulus.
For him, in whose womanish heart fears stand,
that hand may move, which, steeped in unspeakable slaughter,
when the Furies sought their penalties, perhaps with his father's
blood, as he died, sealed the wicked verse.'
Then, threatening, in haste he distributes the duties of battle,
and where Nealces, savage, marshals the wild nations and his line,
there he opposes himself with the Marsian soldiery and against
the standards of the Samnites and the Iapygian nursling.
But in the middle of the field (for in this part he saw
the leader of Libya stand) Servilius is bidden to go to meet
the arms and to lead on the Picentes and the Umbrians.
The rest of the contests Paulus holds on the right wing.
Above these, to go against the ambushes and the flying band
of the Numidians is granted to the son of Scipio, and he foretells
that the squadrons which by craft and tricks will split themselves
he is to scatter the war among.
And now the battle-lines drew near, and with the nimble running
of men and with mouths made hot at once by the mingled
neighing of the hoofed beasts and the much-clashing arms
a blind murmur wandered through the troubled columns.
So, when the winds first stir contests on the sea,
the wave of the strait brings to birth the rage shut within
and the storms that will scatter the stars, and, moved from its depths,
breathes through the rocks the threatening sounds, and, driven from its caverns,
whirls the panting sea with foaming eddy.
Nor indeed was that toil, in so savage a whirlwind of fate,
of the lands alone. Mad discord
entered heaven and forced the gods to war.
On this side Mavors, on this Apollo, the companion of Gradivus,
and the tamer of the swollen sea fights, on this Venus, distraught,
on this Vesta and, stirred by the slaughter of captured Saguntum,
the son of Amphitryon, and likewise venerable Cybele
and the Indigetes gods and Faunus and the founder Quirinus
and Pollux, alternating his soul with Castor exchanged.
Against them, her side girt with iron, Saturnian Juno
and Pallas, born of the Tritonian's Libyan waters,
and ancestral Hammon, his horns bent over his temples,
and a great throng besides of the lesser gods.
When at the mass of them coming together and at their steps the kindly
earth trembled, part filled the neighbouring mountains,
divided, part took their seat beneath a high cloud:
the descent to battle was made through the empty sky.
A measureless shout is raised to the deserted stars,
as great as the voices the earth-born army poured to the air
on the Phlegraean plains, or as the new thunderbolts
Jupiter, the sower of the ages, demanded of the Cyclopes with great voice,
when he saw the great-souled Giants go, with mountains heaped up,
to seize the heavenly realms.
Nor indeed in such great clashes was there any
first spear: a shrieking cloud, with the rage of weapons
contending, was poured forth at once, and the souls, greedy
of blood, fell on this side and that in a twin storm.
And before the mad sword is drawn by the right hand,
a great part of the fighters lies low. Over the very bodies
of their own they stand, eager, and trample on the groaning.
And no more can the Dardanian manhood be thrust forth
or turned away by the Libyan effort, nor can the Sarranian band,
fixed in its rank, be driven, than if the sea
should begin to tear Calpe from its seat with its hurled flood.
They have lost the room for a blow, nor, with death accomplished,
can they fall, hemmed in. The helmet, grim, blazes
at the clash of the opposing helmet, and the shield gapes
at the push of a shield, and sword is bruised by sword.
Foot is worn by foot, and man by man, and the earth cannot
be seen, covered with blood, and a dense night, hanging
beneath the air with weapons heaped on, took away the sky and the stars.
Those whom Fortune had granted to stand in a favourable place
with the long blow of the pike and the tall point,
as if they drove the front lines, mingle their contests.
But those whom an inglorious rank holds behind,
strive with missiles to equal the battles of those before them.
Beyond, the shout drives the war, and the soldier, lacking
the Mars he longs for, urges on the foe with savage cries.
No kind of weapon is wanting. These rouse battles
with the stake, these with the blazing pine, these with the weight of the javelin,
but another with stones and the sling and the flying dart.
At times the shrieking reed is borne through the clouds,
at times the firebrand-spear, to be feared by the very walls.

title: Punica
text:
Do we hope, goddesses, whose sacred rites are tended by me,
that we can open out this whole day, with a mortal voice,
to the ages? Do you grant me so much to trust to my tongue
that I should sound Cannae with one mouth? If our glory
pleases you and you do not turn away from great daring,
hither summon all song and Phoebus the father.
But would, henceforth, Roman, that you might bear favouring fortune
in such spirit as you now bear adverse, and let them be, I pray, thus far,
nor let it please the gods to try whether the Trojan offspring
can endure an equal war. And you, anxious for your fate,
lay aside, I beg, your tears, and worship the wounds that will bring you
perpetual praises. For at no time, Rome,
will you be greater. Soon you will so slip in prosperity
that you preserve by fame the names of your disasters alone.
And now Fortune, alternating among the various changes
of fortune on both sides, had mocked their angers with an uncertain
outcome, and, with the hope of both nations long hanging in the midst,
Mavors blazed amid the matched arms:
as when gentle breezes stir the green stalks,
and the wind does not yet drive the ears that are not yet ripe,
hither and thither the top of the crop goes, and, nodding in turn
with alternate motion, gleams, slowly bent.
At last Nealces, charging with a sharp shout, scatters the line
broken by the barbarian forces.
The wedges were loosened, and through the gaps, hastened on,
the foe burst upon the alarmed. Then in a black whirlwind
a torrent of blood overflows, and no body falls
beneath a single point. While the Ausonian warrior
fears wounds in the back, he catches the savage deaths
in his breast and wards off disgrace from his death.
There stood among the foremost in the contest of the middle battle,
ever loving the harsh and equal to any peril,
Scaevola, and now he did not wish for life amid so great a slaughter,
but a death worthy of his forefather and a dying under a name.
He, after he saw that things were broken and that destruction
grew, said: 'Let us extend whatever brief space of life is left;
for valour is an idle name,
unless the times of a glorious death be enough in the bearing.'
He spoke, and into the midst, where the roused right hand of the Carthaginian
drives a path, straining, he is borne with a vast whirlwind.
Here he comes upon Caralis, exulting and wishing to put on
the snatched gear from a slain man's lofty trunk,
with his sword, and drove the iron in, in anger, up to the hilt.
That man rolls, falling, and at the hostile fields with his bite
he snatches and presses the pangs of death into the earth.
Nor did the raging hands of Gabar and Siccha hold back
their man with united valour; but keen Gabar lost,
while he stood, his right hand, cut off amid the battles;
and Siccha, while, with great grief troubling him,
he rashly hastens aid, unforeseeing trod on a sword
and fell, and too late condemned the steps of his bare
foot, and lies by the right hand of his dying friend.
At last the swelling fury of the youth turned the fatal weapons
of lightning-like Nealces. He leaps forth, burning,
with so famous a name goading him toward the prizes of slaughter.
Then a flint, torn from a crag, which the torrent had brought down
from the high mountains, he snatches and, turbid, whirls into his face.
The jaws cracked at the dashed weight,
and the face was carried away from the man: the gore
flows through the nostrils with the bloody brain congealed, and black
the eyes drip from their crushed sockets and the maimed lights from the forehead.
Marius is laid low, having tried to succour his like-souled
Caper, and fearing to survive the man as he fell.
The same beginning of life, the same fatherland, and common to the two
their poverty: the youths, born at sacred Praeneste,
had mingled their pursuits and sowed on shared land.
The same was their to-wish and not-to-wish, and a mind allied
through all their life, and a concord rich in little things.
They fell together, and of all their prayers this one
Fortune granted, a death joined in the midst of battle.
The twin arms were a glory to the victor Symaethus.

title: Punica
text:
But it was not allowed the Carthaginians to rejoice long
in so great a gift of chance. With menacing terror was at hand
Scipio, pitying the backs of the cohort turned in flight,
and Varro, the source of all the evil, and yellow-haired
Curio and Brutus, descended from the first consul.
And the line, propped by these men, would have repaired the lost
field with a new mass, had not the Carthaginian leader
suddenly with a whirlwind curbed his columns now running forward.
And he, when he saw Varro afar amid the battles
and the lictor flying around him with his red cloak:
'I know the pomp, and I know the insignia.
Such was Flaminius lately,' he said. Then, hot, the keen
anger of his huge shield he foretells with a thunder.
Alas, wretched man! You could have been made equal in death to Paulus,
had it not then, by the gods' anger, been taken from you
to have fallen by Hannibal's hand. How often will you complain,
Varro, to the gods, that you fled the Sidonian sword!
For Scipio, bearing in death a sudden safety with his rapid
charge, †turned upon himself the dangers begun.
Nor does it grieve the Carthaginian, though the honour
of a rich slaughter is snatched away, to have changed his battle
for a greater foe, and at the Ticinus's streams to exact
the penalties for his snatched father, the contest at last offered.
They stood, brought forth on different shores of the world,
such as no other land had seen meet,
equal in Mars and right hand, but in the rest the Latin leader
went before, better in piety and faith.
They leaped down to the troubled battle from a hollow cloud,
Mavors fearing for the son of Scipio, the Tritonian for the Carthaginian,
and at the coming of the gods both battle-lines
trembled, their leaders undaunted. Black, where Pallas turns
her breast, the fire flashes far and wide from the Gorgon's face,
and the aegis twists its hissings with horrid serpents.
Bloody, so that you would believe a twin comet quivered,
gleam her eyes, and on the top of her helmet a generous
crest rolls its waving flames to the stars.
But Mavors, driving the air before with his weapon brandished
and wrapping the field in his shield, wears the breastplate
that pours out Aetnean fires by the gift of the Cyclopes,
and beats the air, rising with his tawny crest.
The leaders, intent on battle, and having measured more closely
how much each in turn would dare, yet perceived
that the arms-bearing gods had come, and, each glad
to be watched by the gods, added wraths to their minds.
And now Pallas with her right hand had twisted aside
the spear, poised with a strong blow from the Carthaginian's breast,
and Gradivus, taught by the example to bring aid
to the fierce goddess, straightway held out the Aetnean
sword to the youth for the battles and bade him greater things.
Then the Virgin, kindling deep within, violent, suddenly
flooded her face with flames, and twisting her sidelong
eyes, surpassed the Gorgon with her troubled visage.
All the monstrous water-snakes raised their huge limbs,
the aegis being shaken, and at the blows of her first frenzy
Mavors himself drew back his foot by degrees from the contest.
Here the goddess, with a swift effort, hurls a torn part
of the neighbouring mountain and rocks bristling with crags
at Mars, raging, and Sason, its shore shaken, took fright
at the sounds carried far back.
But these battles did not deceive the king of the gods.
He quickly sends down Iris, girded with clouds,
to curb the excessive movements, and speaks thus:
'Go, goddess, and swiftly glide to the Oenotrian lands,
and tell my sister to soften her fierce angers
and not to hope to overturn the fixed laws of the Parcae.
Tell her too: ''If you do not desist (for I know the venom and heat
of your flame-bearing mind) and do not gather in your anger,
you shall learn how far the dread thunderbolts excel the aegis.'''
After the Tritonian maiden, hesitating, received this,
nor for long sure enough whether to yield to her father's arms:
'We will withdraw,' she said, 'from the field. But with Pallas driven off,
will he turn aside the fates? And will he keep me from the high heaven
from seeing the fields of Garganus seething with slaughter?'
Having spoken thus, she bore the Carthaginian, lifted in a hollow
cloud, away from the contests, and left the lands.

title: Punica
text:
But fierce Gradivus, at the departure of the goddess returning
to the air, recalls the minds, and those scattered over the plain
he himself with his great hand, wrapped in keen mist,
restores to the battle. The Italians turn their standards and renew,
their fear reversed, a new slaughter.
The keeper set over the winds, whose breaths the prison
holds compressed by his command, and to whom heaven and the rushing
East winds and the North obey, and the West winds and the South,
at the prayers of Juno, who brought no small promises,
unbridles for the battles, on the Aetolian plains, the reigning
Vulturnus. This avenger of her destroying anger pleases her.
He, after he plunged himself into the white pit of Aetna
and conceived fires and brought forth a flaming face,
flies out with a horrendous shriek, and the Daunian realms
he blows through, driving a blind cloud of gathered dust.
The gusts snatched away their eyes and their voice and their hands.
With its sandy white whirl, lamentable to tell,
it whirls balls of it into the faces of the Italians, and rejoices
in the frenzy bidden to war with the companies. Then by the mass of ruin
both soldier and arms and trumpets are laid low on the earth,
and every lance is carried backward, the blast meeting it,
and on the Rutulians the blow falls vainly on their backs.
And the same blast favours the weapons of the Carthaginians,
and, like spears hurled with a throwing-strap, the whirlwind
helps and, shrieking, drives on the Tyrian spears.
Then the soldier, his throat closed with dense dust,
mourns his coward death with his gaping mouth choked.
He himself, his yellow head hidden in the black gloom,
Vulturnus, and his hair drenched with much sand,
now drives those turned from behind with his shrieking wings,
now, coming against their faces in the centre, with the screaming storm
shakes their arms before them and hisses with his open mouth.
At times those intent on battle and now, now on the point of bearing
the steel to the enemy's throat with effort and blow,
he turns aside and tears the right hand from the very wound.
Nor is it enough to befoul the Ausonian cohorts far and wide:
he vomits into the war the air mingled with bellowings,
and twice with his whirlwind he made the topmost crests of the god quiver.
While the Aeolian fury wages these battles against the Roman
squadrons and kindles Mars into wrath,
the Virgin, with Juno as ally, addresses her father:
'How great a flood Gradivus drives into the Punic camp,
look, and with how great slaughters, raging, he fills himself!
Now, I beg, does it not please you that Iris descend to the lands?
Although I came not to destroy the Trojans (since with our pledge
Rome reigns, and I set my seat with the Palladium in this city),
not to destroy the Trojans, but I refused that the light of her
nursling Libya, Hannibal, be driven from life in his flowering years
and that beginnings so great be extinguished.'
Here Juno takes her up, and from the anger of her long toil:
'Nay,' she said, 'that the nations may know how much the measureless
realms of Jove avail and how much your power, husband,
stands before all the gods, scatter with your blazing
weapon (we ask nothing else) the citadels of Carthage,
and plunge the Sidonian line, in a vast chasm of the earth,
into the Tartarean depths, or overwhelm it with the sea.'
Against this Jupiter answers with gentle face:
'You contend with the fates and stretch out sickly hopes.
He, O daughter, to whom you gladly bore hostile weapons,
that youth shall crush the Tyrians and put on the name of the race
and carry the Libyan laurel to the Capitol.
But he to whom you, wife, give spirit and glory,
(I sing the fates) shall turn his arms away from the Laurentine peoples.
Nor are the bounds of disaster far off. The hour and the day comes
on which he shall wish he had crossed no Alps at all.'
So he says, and quickly sends Iris down from Olympus
to recall Mars and bid him withdraw from the battle.
Nor, having struggled against the prohibition, did Gradivus go off into the high
clouds without a roar, though the war-horns and trumpets
and wounds and blood and shouting and arms gave him joy.

title: Punica
text:
When at last the field lay open, free of the gods' contest,
and loosed of the god, the Carthaginian rushes from the lowest part of the plain,
whither he had gradually fled from the heavenly arms,
drawing with a great voice both horse and men and the mass
of the wild turret-bearing beast and the labours of the engines.
And when he recognized the youth, troubling the troops with his lighter
sword, and his anger sparkled on his bloody
cheeks: 'What Furies or what god,' he said, 'drove you against the foe,
see, Minucius, that you should dare again to entrust yourself to us?
Your father, born of my arms, where is your Fabius now? Once, shameless one,
let it be enough to have escaped our hands.' And then,
the spear, companion to his proud words, with a wall-breaking whirlwind
pierces through his breast and forestalls his coming words with the blow.
Nor is it enough to rage with the iron. The wild beast is brought up
with its black mass, and the Italian manhood is matched against the monsters.
For, riding ahead on his horse, he bids the Moor who guides
the Lucanian oxen into war with his goad to drive on with greater spurs
and to whirl on the herds of the Libyan beasts.
Hugely shrieking it is driven, and, compelled by frequent
wound, the warlike beast bears its hasty steps.
On its livid back sits a tower armed with flame and men
and javelins. From afar the rough hail
of stones falls upon the arms, and far and wide the Libyan, lofty,
pours a flying cloud of weapons from the mound.
A long rampart stands, crowded through the close columns,
with snow-white tusks, and, fixed at close quarters to the ivory, a spear
gleams, its point directed from the curved tip.
Here, amid the alarms of the moment, through limbs, through arms,
the beast drives its wicked tusk into Ufens
and bears him, crying out, carried over the trampled columns.
Nor was Tadius's death lighter: where his breastplate
of many-folded linen closes his side, by degrees the wicked
points of the tusk pierced, his body unhurt,
and bore the man aloft, his shield resounding.
His valour was not shaken off by the terror of the new peril:
he uses the chance for glory, and, near, with his swift sword
pierces through the twin light before its brow.
Goaded by the heavy wound, the beast lifts itself to the air
and, with its legs raised, casts off and hurls the tower far
behind, rolling with its weight bent back.
Arms and men together and the beast, robbed of its sight,
are laid low in a sudden ruin, pitiable, mingled.
Against the fighting monsters the Dardanian leader bids
blazing torches be scattered, and the walls which the beast
carries about to be filled with the sulphur of the black brand.
Nor was there delay at the command. The smoking backs of the elephants
gleam with the gathered flames, and the devouring fire, snatched
by the sounding wind, is borne through the bulwarks.
No otherwise, when a shepherd casts fires on Pindus or Rhodope,
and the burning plague ranges through the woods,
the leafy crags catch fire, and suddenly through the high
ridges the Vulcanian blaze gleams, leaping abroad.
The beast goes, its body glowing with white-hot pitch,
distraught, and parts the squadrons with a wide path.
Nor has anyone valour to take up closer battle:
they dare with far-off javelins and the blow of the reed.
It burns, impatient, and with the heat of its great body
the beast, casting flames hither and thither, kindles them,
until at last it threw itself headlong into the waves
of a neighbouring river, and, deceived by the thin liquid,
through the levels of the standing shoal it bore, driven on,
the flame towering from the long banks. Then at last
it plunged its mass, the deep receiving it, into the gulf.

title: Punica
text:
But where battle is given, and not yet is the Maurusian plague
hot with fire, the Rhoetean manhood, poured around,
now with javelins, now with stones, now with winged lead
assail it from afar, like those who storm fortresses
fortified through high places and besiege citadels.
Daring deeds worthy of the man, worthy of favouring fortune,
the unlucky Mincius had raised his right hand and his sword
close against it in his daring; but the beast, shrieking,
breathing out its panting heat, took away his hand
with its keen coil, entangled in a knot, and twisted it with a dire bond,
and, hurling the wretched man high through the upper air,
dashed him to the earth, lamentable, with his limbs crushed.
Amid these disasters, Varro being seen beneath arms,
Paulus, upbraiding him: 'Why do we not go close,' he said,
'against the Tyrian leader, whom we promised the city
would stand bound, his neck in chains, before your chariot?
Alas, fatherland, alas, commons wicked and crooked in favour!
Never in so hard a lot of evils will you make out
which it should rather have been your prayer never to have been born to you,
Varro or Hannibal.' While Paulus says such things,
the Libyan presses the headlong and against the backs of those rushing
before his eyes rouses all the spears of the leader.
The helmet is beaten and the consul's arms are shaken.
The keener for this, Paulus, fierce, rushes into the midst of the foe.
But then Varro, his mind struck from him, turned, with Paulus
drawn away into trackless contests, and bending his steed
with his hand: 'You pay the penalties, fatherland,' he said,
'who, with Fabius unharmed, called Varro to the wars.
But what discord of mind or of fate
and what hidden trick of the Parcae is there? Long since
it pleases me to break off all things together with the light. But some
god or other holds back my sword. But for what graver things he keeps me!
Shall I live? And shall I carry these broken fasces, scattered
with the blood of my own, back to the people, and shall I give my face
to be gazed on through the angry cities, and—what Hannibal
himself would scarcely demand more savagely—shall I flee and see you, Rome?'
As he protested more, the foes drove him on with closer
weapons, and his steed, the reins loosed, snatched him away.
10. Paulus, seeing the unequal battle swell against him,
like a wild beast that, when weapons ring it round, leaps
of its own will onto the steel and gathers the foe through its wounds,
carries his arms into the thickest crowds and flings himself
on danger, and from every blade contrives his death.
Terribly he cries: 'Stand fast and bravely, I beg you,
take the steel in your breasts, and carry your backs
unwounded down to the shades, men. If not the glory of death,
nothing is left. To you, going down to the lowest seats,
the same Paulus here will be your leader.' From there more swiftly
than the Thracian north wind, faster than the feathered shaft
that the fleeing Parthian sends back into the fight from his reed,
and where Cato, forgetful of his early years,
his mind brimming with the war god, stirs the foremost combat,
he is borne against the enemy
and from deadly arms snatches a youth whom the light-armed
Vascon, whom the Cantabrian thick with javelins, was pressing.
They drew back, and, turned in terrified retreat,
withdrew their steps: as, glad in a distant valley,
when a hunter drives a doe and presses the spent quarry
in close pursuit and hopes already to touch it with his hand,
if a fierce lion has thrust itself, sudden, from the cave before it
and stood gnashing before his eyes: at once there desert him
his colour and his blood, and his weapons, too small for the peril,
and no care for the hoped-for prey remains in his breast.
Now he drives his sword-point at close quarters against those who stand,
now with his weapons he overtakes the trembling who have turned
their backs in evil dread. To rage, and to grace his labours,
and to be savage, delights him. A vast nameless throng
falls to one man, and, were a second Paulus given
to the Dardan arms, Cannae would lose its name.

title: Punica
text:
At last, the wing broken, the front line rushed
in disorder, not sparing flight. Labienus and Ocres
are laid low in death, and Opiter, whom Setia sent from her
vine-clad hill, and Labienus whom the lofty rocks of Cingulum
sent from their high walls. The Sidonian soldier
met the cruel hour of death, though not by like fortune:
for Labienus dies, the cornel-spear piercing through his groin,
and brothers fell, this one struck in the shoulder, that in the knee.
You too fall, Maecenas, pinned above the loins by a Tyrian dart,
you to whom the Maeonian land gave a name revered
and once renowned among the Etruscan sceptres.
Through the midst, his love of light cast off,
Paulus is driven, seeking out Hannibal. One lot alone seems
bitter to him: to fall while the Punic leader still lives.
Fearing that catastrophe (for surely, once the contest were joined,
no storm so great, no fury, would have gone unpunished),
Juno, changed into the likeness of timid Metellus,
said: 'Why, sole hope of Latium, consul,
do you stir empty and vain frenzies while fate refuses?
If Paulus survives, the realm of Aeneas remains;
but if not, you drag Ausonia down with you. To go
against that swelling youth and to cut off this life
amid such ruin, Paulus, do you make ready? Now Hannibal
(so glad is he in war) would dare to fight the Thunderer himself.
And already, with reins reversed (for I saw him wheel),
Varro has escaped and keeps himself for better things.
Let there be room for fate, and, while it is granted, snatch from death
this soul, greater than ours: soon you will take up the war again.'
To this the leader, sighing: 'Why I should ask for death
in arms—is that cause too slight, that our ears
have borne with Metellus urging such monstrous counsel?
Go, madman, go, take to flight. May the gods grant
you do not catch the enemy's weapons in your back, I pray.
Unhurt, I beg, untouched may you depart, and enter the walls
of Rome together with Varro. Coward, did you think
me worthy of such a life, unworthy of a noble death?
No doubt the Punic allows it—he who now has strength
to wage a contrary war against Jove himself. Oh degenerate
from the high virtue of our fathers! When could I enter combat,
or with what man would I rather match myself, than one
who in defeat and in victory alike will give a name through the ages?'
With such words he upbraids him and is borne into the midst of the foe,
and Acherras, bending his course back toward the thronging
ranks of his own and stealing his limbs away into the dense maniples,
through the crowded press of men and shields packed close,
he overtakes with swifter foot and cuts down,
as when a Belgic hound hunts the hidden boars,
and, skilled, tracks the beast's wanderings through trackless ground,
his nose buried, and pressing the trail with silent snout
ranges the glens unreached by the hunters' nets,
nor stops, until, following the scent he has caught,
he finds the secret lair in the thick brambles.
But the consort of Jove, when driving Paulus off with words
proved useless, and the consul did not cease from his wrath,
changed again into the shape of Moorish Gelestes,
calls the Punic, unaware, away from the savage fight:
'Here turn your weapons, here,' she says, 'bring your right hand
to those who implore it, eternal glory of Carthage. Close by,
the consul is mounting a grim battle along the standing pools
of the riverbank, and no greater fame is won
by any other foe brought down.' So she speaks
and hurries the youth off to another quarter of the fight.

title: Punica
text:
On the river's bank one was harrying the Libyan band—
Crista was his name. Twice three sons, joined,
bore arms about the old man; poor in his household
(yet his house, Tuder, was not obscure, and he was known
through the Umbrian peoples, a warrior) by his deeds and slaughter
he taught his band of weapon-bearing sons to handle battle.
That single-minded phalanx, with their harsh master leading,
after it was sated with the death of men, had laid low with countless blows
a wild beast bearing a tower, and, the torches following,
watched gladly the burning monster's downfall,
when a sudden flash of a helmet, and crests bristling
from a taller cone, made them shudder. Old age was not slow
(for by the gleam he knew the man): the savage parent
seizes his sons from the line, of his own will, into the fray,
and bids them hurl their darts on every side and not to dread
the flames that streamed from the fierce mouth
or those that blazed from the helmet.
Even so the armour-bearer of mighty Jove, when in the anxious nest
he nurtures fledglings worthy to carry the thunderbolt,
watching the brood with faces turned toward Phaethon's chariot,
tests his doubtful young against the lamp of Phoebus.
And now, to give the proofs of battle to his own as he called them
. . .
and the swift spear flits past through the empty air.
The point lodged, not deep, in the layered gold
and, hanging slack, betrayed his age by its feeble stroke.
To him the Punic: 'What madness drove a hand drained
by old age to a vain blow? Scarcely did the trembling cornel
of Callaican metal bite my outer covering.
See, I return your weapons to you: from us
that memorable youth of yours will better learn to wage war.'
So with his own spear he transfixes the wretch's breast.
But in answer, dreadful to see, twice three darts fly,
hurled by his right hand, and the spears rush with equal effort:
just as when a hunter, a Moor, presses a lioness
that has lately whelped on Libyan soil, besieged in her cave,
the cubs, long since raging, rush in and make vain trials
of combat with teeth not yet firm enough.
With his shield the Sidonian leader spends their darts,
and, gathered into his arms, withstands
the pressing spears with their clattering blows,
nor does he think enough has yet been done by all these wounds
or all this slaughter, and he pants with rage
unless he gives all the men to death and joins their bodies
to the father's and uproots the wretched house with its stock.
Then he addresses Abaris (for he, the armour-bearer, with one wrath
kindled his war-spirit and went as comrade in his every act):
'Supply me with weapons. That throng longs to be sent down
to the pools of livid Avernus, the throng that assails
my shield: now it shall have the fruit of its foolish loyalty.'
So saying, with his javelin he pierces Luca, the eldest,
through; the youth, sinking under the pressing point,
falls back with face upturned upon his brothers' arms.
Then Volso, hurrying with his hand to wrench the deadly steel,
he lays low with a pilum (for chance was offering this
from the heap of the slain), driving it home through the covering nostril.
Then Vesulus, slipping in the warm blood of his brothers,
he reaps with swift sword and (alas, barbarous valour!)
the helmet of the severed head, like a missile weapon,
he flings at those who had turned their backs. Telesinus, his bones
crushed by a hurled stone where the spine binds the limbs,
falls, and sees the sinking body of his brother
Quercens, whom a sling-stone, whirled from afar through the void,
had stunned, while Telesinus into the air
breathes out his last light and closes his wavering eyes.
But Perusinus, worn alike by grief and running and fear,
yet not free of wrath, was bearing his uncertain limbs
unsteadily across the plain, halting at times.
Him, with a stake that the armour-bearer had torn
from the back of the fallen Libyan monster and offered,
fixed above his loins, the Sidonian cuts down
and violently presses with the fire-hardened oak.
He had tried with prayers to soften the savage fury,
but the Stygian heat had filled his first gasps,
and down to the lung his breath drew in the fire.
At last, fallen with all his flock, a name long
famous among the Umbrian folk, Crista: as when a tall
ilex, or an oak known from its founders' ancestral line,
smokes, struck by the lightning for Jove, and through the years
the flames lay waste its sacred boughs with heavenly sulphur,
until, conquered by the god, it sinks wide on the ground
and, collapsing, buries all its progeny under the spreading trunk.

title: Punica
text:
And while the Tyrian leader works at this beside the Aufidan pools,
Paulus, having now avenged by numberless slaughter
the death to come, waged war as though a victor.
Among a thousand men lies huge Phorcys, from the caves
of Herculean Calpe, his shield engraved with the Gorgon,
from whom his stock and his grim origin † flowed from the goddess.
Him, as he flung himself forward and swelled with the ancient
monstrous names of stone-making Medusa's line,
while leaning in more fiercely he aims at the left groin,
Paulus drags down, seizing him by the crest of his lofty cone,
and, pressing him to the ground where the belt at its lowest
curves on the back and sits as guard to either hip,
he stabs him above with thrust sword: the other vomits a warm
stream of blood, pouring it through his gaping vitals,
and that dweller of Atlas sinks into the Aetolian fields.
Amid this carnage, roused in a sudden terror,
men attack the rear and with a reversed whirlwind mingle
unlooked-for battle—men whom the Tyrian had trained,
skilled to deceive, for this very stratagem of war,
the commander himself, and, girded with guile,
as if they were fleeing the Punic camp,
had surrendered their hands. Then with all their hearts
they hurl behind the line driven into slaughter,
rushing upon their backs. Neither spear fails the man, nor sword:
the steel is from the slaughter, the weapons wrenched from corpses.
Galba, when from afar he saw the standard
carried off by the foe (for adversity has no power
to take away the love of valour), straining with his whole body,
overtakes the victor and seizes him with a deadly stroke.
And while he was tearing the captured spoil from the slain body,
and his dying hand loosed its grip too slowly,
he fell, run through by the sword of Amorgus rushing up,
dying, not blessed in his great venture.
Meanwhile, as if Enyo had not yet glutted
her savage furies, the Volturnus whirls the field
lifted in dust and hurls the gleaming sands.
And now, shrieking monstrously, the storm carried
the struggling men far across the field to its farthest edge
and, dashed against the hollow banks, plunged them into the swollen river.
Here was your end, here Aufidus kept for you the bounds
of life, ill-starred Curio, in a silent death.
For, raging in spirit, while he holds back the panic-stricken
ranks and strives to stem them with his body in their way,
hurled headlong by the great mass of those who rush,
he is swallowed in the troubled waters and, rolled along the bottom,
lay on the Adriatic sand, his death without a name.
Unable to bear great evils or to bow his neck to Fortune,
the consul charged against the conquering arms with face set forward:
a warlike ardour to die, and now only
the confidence of death, gave him spirit,
when Viriathus, driving with his darts, the great-souled
ruler of the Spanish land, near and before the face
of the raging Paulus, cuts down his foe, spent with the fight.
Alas, the grief, alas the tears! Servilius, best in war—
after Paulus, war's best part—falls by a barbarian
stroke, and dying added by one death great
odium to Cannae. The consul did not endure the bitter wrath,
and, though the violence of the mad winds disarms him
with their opposing force and veils the light with dust,
breaking grim through the heaped sand's squalor
he enters the storm and assails Viriathus,
who poured forth barbarous songs in the Spanish fashion,
beating his shield, and pierced the vitals of his left breast.
This was the last labour of his killing. No further
might his hand add to the war, nor, Rome, was Paulus
left to you for the battles hereafter.
A huge stone, hurled with vast weight, by an unseen hand
came against his face, and, driving the bronze of the shattered helmet
into his bones, filled his features with blood.
Then, drawing back his foot, he laid his sinking limbs
on a nearby crag, and, gasping with the welling wound,
sat down, terrible, over his shield, his face bloodied:
as a monstrous lion, when the lighter spears are driven off,
has at last taken the steel through his breast,
stands, enduring the weapon, trembling in the midst of the sand,
and, as blood streams from his mane and jaws and nostrils,
at times rolling out faint growls,
pours from his wide mouth the foaming gore.
Then indeed the Libyans press on, and over them their leader
himself on his galloping horse, wherever the wind's blast drives,
wherever a path lies open to the sword,
wherever the steed, wherever with warlike tooth the fierce beast.
Here Piso, buried under weapons, when through the bodies of the slain
he saw the lord of Libya, straining on his spear,
pierces the belly of the war-horse with point raised,
and tries, in vain, to fall upon it as it collapses,
when the Punic, quickly gathering his body, though
the steed had thrown him forward, headlong over the bent shoulder:
'Do the ghosts of Ausonia renew, brought back to life,
their wars after death, and not even in death keep still?'
So he speaks, and as the other tries to raise his weakened body,
rising high above him, he buried the whole sword in him.

title: Punica
text:
Behold, his foot wounded by a Cydonian arrow,
Lentulus was leaving the field, his reins let loose,
when he sees Paulus on the crag, bedewing the rocks with blood,
sinking with grim gaze down into Tartarus.
His mind reeled, and he was ashamed of flight. Then Rome
seemed to the man to be burning, then at the gates
bloodstained Hannibal already to stand; then for the first time
before his eyes were the Aetolian fields drinking up Latium.
'What then is left, why should tomorrow's light not lead
the Tyrians to the city, if you abandon the ship,
Paulus, in such storms? I call the gods to witness,' he said,
'unless you steer the losses of this cruel war and live,
against your will, in so great a whirlwind, more, Paulus—
grief dictates these harsh words—more than Varro you do harm.
Take, I beg, this horse, sole hope of our exhausted fortunes.
I myself will lift your failing limbs upon my shoulders
and set you safe on its back.'
Meanwhile, spitting out the blood that streamed from his torn mouth,
the consul: 'Bravo, O worthy of your father's valour!
Nor are our hopes truly narrow, when such hearts
remain to the Romulean realm. Bear off the horse
with your spurs, where the wound allows, and from here quickly
let the city's gates be shut (this plague will rush against those walls);
tell them, I beg: let the reins of state be handed to Fabius.
My fury fought against our own counsels. What more is left
for me to do with my life, but to show the blind crowd
that Paulus knows how to die? Shall I be carried into the city,
spent with wounds? At what price would Hannibal wish to buy it,
to see us turn our backs? Such a heart is not Paulus's,
nor do I enter the shades so small a phantom.
That man I—but why, sick as I am, do I delay you
with vain lament, Lentulus? Go, and with your spear
raise the weary horse quickly.' Then Lentulus seeks the city,
bearing great commands. Nor does Paulus leave unavenged
what is left of his life: as a tiger, yielding at last
to a deadly wound, its body cast down,
wrestles with death and opens its faint jaws
to vain bites, and, its blows not sufficient for its rage,
licks with its last tongue the hunting-spears.
And now, against Ierta, who brandished his weapon and brought
his step nearer, exulting and careless of the slaughter,
he had, rising, fixed his unexpected sword,
and looked round for the Sidonian leader, longing
to lay down his soul striving in that right hand.
But weapons gathering on every side overcame the man—
Numidian and Garamantian and Celt and Moor and Asturian.
This was Paulus's end. There lies a lofty heart and a mighty
right hand, whom, if wars were given to him alone to wage,
you might perhaps have matched with Fabius. To the city his death
gave noble glory and sent his name among the stars.
After the hopes and the minds of the Italians fell with the consul,
the army, as a trunk without its head, is laid low
by cruel arms, and victorious Africa roars across the whole field.
Here the ranks of Picenum, here warlike Umbria, there
the Sicanian youth sinks down, here a Hernican squadron.
Everywhere lie the standards that the warlike Samnite, and those
that the Sarrastian peoples and the Marsian cohorts bore.
Shields pierced through, and helmets, and useless steel,
and coverings of bucklers broken in the clash, and foaming bits
torn from the mouths of the fierce war-horses.
Bloody Aufidus casts its swollen waves upon the plains
and, raging, gives back its own bodies to the banks.
So a Lagean ship, like an island sighted on the vast sea,
when the cloud-bringing east wind has dashed it on the rocks,
scattering wreckage covers the straits: and now through the waves
float thwarts and mast and broken stern-ornaments with torn sail,
and the wretched sailors, vomiting up the sea.

title: Punica
text:
But the Punic, having measured the day through long combats
with savage slaughter, after the darkness snatched from his fury
the notable light, then at last dismissed
the war god and spared his own men in the killing.
Yet his mind keeps watch in its cares and cannot bear
the night's repose. Amid such gifts of the gods it goads him
that he has not yet entered the longed-for gates of Quirinus.
The next dawn pleases him. Hence he resolves to bear swords
drawn at once, while the blood is hot and the cohorts steeped in slaughter,
and now in his mind he seizes the barriers, now the walls with flame,
and joins the burning of the Tarpeian rock to Cannae.
Troubled by this design of the man, Juno, daughter of Saturn,
not ignorant of Jove's wrath and of Latium's fate,
prepares to curb the youth's reckless ardour and his greedy hopes
toward a futile vow. She summons then Sleep,
who reigns in the quiet darkness, by whose ministry she often
soothes the unwilling eyes of her conquered brother to rest,
and, smiling at him: 'Not for greater deeds,
god, do I call you, nor ask that on your soft wings
you give me, Sleep, a conquered Jove. You need not press
a thousand eyes, nor is your power scorned by a guard,
the watcher of the Inachian heifer, to be overcome by long night.
On the Punic leader, I pray, send strange dreams,
that he may not now long to look on Rome and the forbidden walls,
which the ruler of Olympus will never grant him to enter.'
Swift he carries out the command, and winged through the darkness
bears the drugged poppies in his curving horn.
But when, gliding through the silence, he reached the first tents
of the Barcaean youth, then he shakes his slumbrous wings
above the bowed head and sprinkles rest upon his eyes,
touching his temples with the Lethean wand.
Grim, fierce dreams torment his raging mind.
And now it seemed to him that with a great host he girded
the Tiber and, exulting, stood at the walls of Rome.
Jupiter himself shone forth on the height of the Tarpeian crag,
hurling blazing thunderbolts from his lifted right hand,
and the broad fields smoked with sulphur,
and blue Anio trembled in its icy waters,
and before his eyes again and again the dreadful
fires quivered. Then a voice poured through the air:
'Glory great enough, O youth, you have grasped at Cannae.
Halt your step: for it will be no more granted you, Punic,
to break into the sacred walls than to cleave our heaven.'
Astonished by the visions and fearing greater wars,
after Juno's commands were fulfilled Sleep leaves him,
nor did the daylight purge his mind of the terrible image.
Amid these stirrings of sleep and empty tumults,
Mago announces that the camp has surrendered through the night
with the rest of the soldiery, and drags off plunder in a full column.
To him, as he promised glad feasts on the Tarpeian summit,
the leader, when the fifth night had brought the day round in its orbit,
hiding the warnings of the gods and his shut-in fear,
pleads his wounds and the strength drained in the savage fight,
and that one should not trust too much in fortune too favourable.
Then the youth, cast down from hope, as if he were bidden
to turn his back from the very walls and carry back the standards:
'By so great an effort,' he said, 'not Rome, as she herself believed,
but Varro was conquered. Why do you abandon such favourable
gifts of war to fate, and delay our homeland?
